claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, non-uniform native oxide layer before exposure.
Heating Q235 steel in air at approximately 250°C for 2 hours will produce a more homogeneous oxide layer.
Heating Q235 steel in air at approximately 250°C for 2 hours will thermally stabilize its oxide layer.
A uniform, defect-minimized oxide layer impedes ionic transport through the oxide.
Reduced ionic transport through the oxide decreases the number or activity of localized anodic dissolution sites.
Decreasing localized anodic dissolution sites suppresses pitting and general corrosion.
Defects in a heterogeneous oxide layer act as preferential sites for corrosion initiation.
The corrosion-promoting effect of oxide defects becomes stronger at elevated temperature because corrosion reaction kinetics increase.
Thermally treated Q235 steel will show a delayed onset of corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel in saline, high-humidity exposure.
Thermally treated Q235 steel will have lower corrosion current density than untreated Q235 steel.
Thermally treated Q235 steel will undergo less corrosion-related weight loss than untreated Q235 steel.
Thermally treated Q235 steel will develop fewer localized pits than untreated Q235 steel.
The predicted protective effects will occur at both approximately 25°C and approximately 80°C.
The oxide-layer protective effect is expected to be significant mainly under combined high-humidity and saline conditions.
The oxide-layer protective effect may not be observable in low-humidity or non-saline environments.
